title: Didactic example — 8-bit image intensity histogram
description: A real didactic example: how to read the intensity histogram of an 8-bit grayscale image, walking through three contrasting cases — a low-key scene, a high-key scene, and a balanced photograph.

data.markdown:
## Image histograms

For an 8-bit grayscale image, every pixel has an intensity value in $\{0, 1, \ldots, 255\}$. An **intensity histogram** counts how many pixels fall into each bin of the intensity range. Photographers and image-processing engineers read it to spot:

- **Underexposure** — most pixels piled up near 0.
- **Overexposure** — most pixels piled up near 255.
- **Low contrast** — pixels clustered in a narrow strip of the range.
- **Clipping** — a sharp spike right at 0 or 255 (information lost to saturation).

The sections below show three histograms with bins of width 32 (so eight bars total).

sections.title: Low-key scene — most pixels are dark

data.markdown: The mass is concentrated at the dark end of the intensity range — typical of a night scene, a backlit subject, or an underexposed photograph. The right tail is small but non-zero, so a few highlights survive. If the leftmost bar were dramatically taller (say, 30 000 instead of 4 200), the image would be clipped to black at the shadows and the lost detail couldn't be recovered.

sections.title: High-key scene — most pixels are bright

data.markdown: The mirror image of the previous case — mass concentrated at the bright end, typical of a snow scene, a white-walled studio, or an overexposed photograph. Same risk in reverse: a tall spike at the rightmost bar means highlights have clipped to white and the lost detail is unrecoverable from this image alone.

The balanced case spreads pixels across the full range with a single broad peak in the midtones. None of the bins is empty (so the image uses its full dynamic range) and neither end is spiking (so nothing is clipped).

:::callout{type="insight" title="Histograms ≠ \"good photos\""}
A flat histogram does not mean a great photograph — silhouettes, low-key portraits, and high-key fashion shots are all artistically valid even though their histograms would make a digital-camera meter complain. The histogram answers "have I lost information at either end?" — the answer to "is this a good photo?" is up to the photographer.
:::
